content: 1. For patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, the outcomes of three-times-weekly drug dosing throughout the treatment duration were compared to daily drug dosing. The outcomes assessed included cure or treatment completion, treatment failure, disease relapse, death, and the development of acquired drug resistance among patients who experienced treatment failure or relapse. The question explored whether intermittent dosing during the continuation phase yields similar outcomes to daily dosing in these patients. 2. Among patients with pulmonary tuberculosis co-infected with HIV, the initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) during tuberculosis treatment was compared to initiating ART after completing tuberculosis treatment. The outcomes evaluated included the incidence of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), mortality, AIDS-defining illnesses or death, treatment success, treatment completion, disease relapse, and adverse drug effects. The goal was to determine whether early initiation of ART improves outcomes compared to late initiation. 3. For pulmonary tuberculosis patients co-infected with HIV, the effectiveness of extending treatment beyond the standard six-month rifampicin-containing regimen was compared to the standard six-month regimen. The outcomes assessed included treatment failure, disease relapse, and death. 4. In patients with tuberculous pericarditis, the use of adjuvant systemic corticosteroid therapy in combination with first-line oral anti-tuberculosis agents was compared to first-line oral agents plus placebo. The outcomes evaluated included mortality, adherence to treatment, and the development of constrictive pericarditis. 5. For patients with tuberculous meningitis, the use of adjuvant systemic corticosteroid therapy alongside first-line oral anti-tuberculosis agents was compared to first-line oral agents plus placebo. The outcomes assessed included cure or treatment completion, survival, remaining disease-free after treatment, acquisition or amplification of drug resistance, smear or culture conversion during treatment, and adverse drug events. 6. In patients with a history of prior treatment with first-line anti-tuberculosis drugs who require re-treatment due to treatment interruption or recurrence, the effectiveness of empiric re-treatment with five first-line drugs (HRZES, WHO Category II regimen) was evaluated. The outcomes assessed included cure or treatment completion, survival, remaining disease-free after treatment, acquisition or amplification of drug resistance, smear or culture conversion during treatment, and adverse drug events. No randomized controlled trials were available for this evaluation; only observational studies (cohort analyses of re-treatment cases) were considered. 7. For tuberculosis patients, interventions to promote adherence to treatment, such as medication monitors, SMS or telephone reminders, social support (educational, psychological, or material), or combinations of these interventions, were compared to routine practice. The outcomes assessed included adherence to treatment (or treatment interruption due to non-adherence), conventional tuberculosis treatment outcomes (cure, treatment completion, failure, relapse, survival, or death), adverse reactions to tuberculosis drugs (severity, type, or organ class), and costs to the patient (including direct medical costs, transportation, and lost wages) and health services. 8. For patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), decentralized treatment and care were compared to care provided solely by specialized drug-resistant tuberculosis centers or teams. The outcomes assessed included adherence to treatment (or treatment interruption due to non-adherence), conventional tuberculosis treatment outcomes (cure, treatment completion, failure, relapse, survival, or death), adverse reactions to tuberculosis drugs (severity, type, or organ class), acquisition or amplification of drug resistance, and costs to the patient (including direct medical costs, transportation, and lost wages) and health services.
